analysis.investment_thesis: Gujarat Pipavav Port is a genuinely sound enterprise — near-zero debt, consistent decade-long earnings, and robust free cash flow — but Mr. Market is asking a price well above what the numbers justify. At INR 161, it trades at roughly 68% above its Graham Number (~INR 96), offering no margin of safety for the disciplined investor.
key_strengths: Near-pristine balance sheet: D/E of 0.02, borrowings just INR 51 Cr vs equity of INR 2,398 Cr
Unbroken 10-year earnings record (2016–2025) with interest coverage ~96x — exactly the financial fortress Graham demands
Consistently positive free cash flow every year (INR 312–417 Cr range), with large financing outflows indicating real dividend returns to shareholders
key_risks: P/B of 3.25 — more than double Graham's ceiling of 1.5; the investor pays INR 3.25 for each rupee of net assets
Revenue CAGR of only 4.6% over nine years does not justify a premium valuation; earnings volatility visible (net profit fell from INR 319 Cr in 2020 to INR 197 Cr in 2022)
Concession-based port business faces regulatory and government-contract renewal risk; a single major customer or policy change can impair earnings sharply
red_flags: Graham Number ≈ INR 96 (EPS ~8.2, BVPS ~49.7) vs. market price INR 161 — stock is ~68% above intrinsic value by this metric
P/E of 17 exceeds Graham's hard ceiling of 15; combined P/E × P/B = 55, well above Graham's maximum product of 22.5
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Gujarat Pipavav Port passes every quality test I demand: a decade of uninterrupted profits, effectively no debt, operating margins of 44%, and free cash flow that reliably covers and returns capital to shareholders. The promoter (AP Møller–Maersk group at 44%) is a credible, long-term infrastructure operator. Interest coverage is a staggering 96× on trivial finance costs, and the balance sheet shows reserves growing steadily to INR 1,915 Cr. For a business of this character, I have no quarrel with management or financial health.

My quarrel is entirely with price. At INR 161, the stock demands a P/B of 3.25 and a P/E of 17 — both above my maximums. The Graham Number, computed from trailing EPS of ~8.2 and book value per share of ~49.7, yields approximately INR 96. The intelligent investor requires a discount to intrinsic value, not a 68% premium. Revenue has compounded at a mere 4.6% annually over nine years; one cannot justify today's price on growth assumptions alone. I would revisit this at INR 90–100, where a genuine margin of safety would exist. Until then, existing holders may sit tight, but no new capital should be committed.
